children: The US Supreme Court on Tuesday declined to hear an appeal by lawyers who were sanctioned over a lawsuit they brought challenging Arizona's voting machines in the run-up to the state's 2022 midterm elections.

Andrew Parker and his firm, Minneapolis-based Parker Daniels Kibort, were ordered to pay $122,000 after a judge found they made "baseless" claims in their lawsuit on behalf of Arizona gubernatorial candidate Kari Lake and former Arizona state representative Mark Finchem.
Parker argued in his petition to the Supreme Court that the sanctions could chill lawyers' ability to assert unpopular or difficult claims.

"The sanctions in this case have grave implications for our justice system and will deter attorneys from bringing creative, aggressive or novel claims of the sort that are often necessary to shape and reshape our legal landscape," the petition said.
Parker and his attorney did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Parker's petition was opposed by the Maricopa County Board of Supervisors, whose members were named as defendants in the lawsuit. Thomas Liddy of the Maricopa County Attorney's Office said the justices had upheld ethical standards in turning away the appeal.

"The First Amendment allows politicians to say whatever they want to voters to get votes. Lawyers are required by the ethical canons to speak to judges with only facts," Liddy said. "The Supreme Court by denying cert, upheld that standard."

Lake and Finchem, Republicans who had sought statewide offices in the 2022 race, had alleged that the state's voting machines were rife with cybersecurity vulnerabilities and sought a court order requiring Arizonians to cast their votes on paper ballots that would be counted by hand.

US District Judge John Tuchi dismissed the lawsuit before the 2022 election, and Lake and Finchem lost their races to their Democratic opponents. Tuchi had held that the candidates' claims relied on "false, misleading, and unsupported factual assertions," and that Parker and his firm "acted at least recklessly in unreasonably and vexatiously multiplying the proceedings."

The San Francisco-based 9th US Circuit Court of Appeals upheld the sanctions in March 2025. The appeals court overturned related sanctions against retired Harvard Law professor Alan Dershowitz, finding he had a limited role in the case.

The Supreme Court on Tuesday declined to hear Parker's challenge to the sanctions without detailing its reasoning. The justices in April 2024 had declined to take up Lake and Finchem's appeal of the dismissal of their case.
